pitfall_name: JS↔WASM linear memory copy on every witness write
what_happens: Witness generation and proof I/O take 2-5x longer than expected, with CPU profiling showing most time in Uint8Array.set or into wasm memory, not in actual proving.
why: The Web model requires structured data to be serialized into the wasm linear memory before calling an exported function. When JS holds canonical witness objects (Uint8Arrays, typed arrays) and the proving library expects raw pointers, every call copies. For FRI/Merkle-heavy proving where witness buffers are megabytes and called many times, this is the dominant cost. The copy is invisible from a single-call microbenchmark because it amortizes over a large compute region, but shows up clearly in a flame graph.
how_discovered: Profiler trace shows 30-60% of wall time inside Uint8Array.prototype.set / TypedArray.copyWithin / DataView.set calls feeding wasm; or a memory.grow print loop showing steady allocation that doesn't match algorithmic allocation. Typical waste: 2-4 engineer-days chasing 'why is the prover slow' before someone looks at the I/O.
mitigation: Allocate a shared scratch region in wasm linear memory once, hand JS a pointer + length, then use Module.HEAPU8.subarray(ptr, ptr+len) for in-place reads/writes. For large witnesses, consider passing handles and copying only at phase boundaries, not per operation. For streaming proofs, use a single growing buffer and pass offsets.

pitfall_name: SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation and breaks embed
what_happens: Threads-enabled wasm module loads but falls back to a single-threaded path silently, or throws 'SharedArrayBuffer is not defined' at module instantiation, or works locally but fails when deployed behind any iframe or with cookies set.
why: SharedArrayBuffer and the wasm threads proposal require the page to be cross-origin isolated: HTTP headers Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (or credentialless) must both be present. Without them, browsers refuse to enable SharedArrayBuffer. CDN-hosted assets, third-party scripts, and any iframe that doesn't send CORP/CORS break the isolation. Some browsers additionally gate on 'site-keyed' cookies or active sign-in.
how_discovered: Works perfectly on localhost, then throws on the deployed URL. Or: proof generation is 4x slower than expected because the threaded path silently fell back. Diagnostic: console shows 'SharedArrayBuffer is not defined' or crossOriginIsolated === false in the devtools console. Typical waste: 1-3 days, often confused with a CDN misconfiguration.
mitigation: Set both COOP and COEP headers at the origin and on every served asset. Audit third-party scripts (analytics, fonts) for COEP compatibility — many break. Use credentialless COEP for third-party image/font hosts. For embed scenarios, document that the host page must also be cross-origin isolated; if it cannot be, do not use threads and design the prover for a single-threaded path with SIMD.

pitfall_name: wasm 32-bit address space exhaustion on large witnesses
what_happens: Module throws RangeError: Out of memory or Cannot enlarge memory arrays mid-proof, or silently but with degraded performance because gc is hammering the heap. Provers targeting >4GB working sets fail outright in browser even though desktop native would handle them.
why: WebAssembly's MVP memory model is a single linear memory with 32-bit pointers and a 4GB ceiling. The memory64 proposal exists and is shipping in some browsers (Chrome behind flag, Firefox later) but is not the default and toolchains (binaryen, wasm-bindgen, Emscripten) may not yet target it without explicit flags. Most existing crypto proving libraries were compiled for wasm32.
how_discovered: Allocation profile shows memory.grow repeatedly requesting large pages near the 2GB mark, then failing. Or: works on a 16GB dev machine, fails in a CI runner with 4GB. Typical waste: half a day to realize it's not a memory leak but the address space ceiling.
mitigation: Target memory64 explicitly when the prover needs >2GB working sets; check toolchain support (latest Emscripten, Rust nightly target wasm64-unknown-unknown). For wasm32 builds, design proving algorithms to operate on memory windows — process large witnesses in chunks with explicit streaming rather than holding the whole trace. Set INITIAL_MEMORY and MAXIMUM_MEMORY explicitly; do not rely on growth at runtime near the ceiling.

pitWorker pool serialization overhead exceeds compute savings
what_happens: Splitting a proving workload across N workers yields no speedup, or is actually slower than single-threaded. Profiling shows most time is in postMessage / structuredClone of witness buffers between workers.
why: Workers do not share linear memory unless SharedArrayBuffer is in play. If the wasm module's memory is not shared, every cross-worker call copies the witness and intermediate state via structuredClone. For FRI/MSM where the witness is hundreds of MB, this copy is the bottleneck — the GPU/CPU compute is hidden behind it. Even with SAB, the JS-side postMessage of typed arrays through a SAB has a measurable copy step when you slice() or .set() into another memory.
how_discovered: Worker pool benchmark with 1, 2, 4, 8 workers shows flat or negative scaling. Chrome DevTools' Performance tab shows long yellow 'Messaging' blocks between threads. Typical waste: 1-2 days.
mitigation: Use SharedArrayBuffer-backed wasm memory across all workers (requires cross-origin isolation). Partition the witness once and assign each worker a non-overlapping slice. Avoid per-step messaging; collect results at phase boundaries only. If SAB is not available, evaluate honestly whether the single-thread SIMD path beats the multi-thread message-passing path for your workload size.

pitfall_name: SIMD codegen claim without actual vectorization of field arithmetic
what_happens: Toolchain reports -msimd128 enabled and the wasm contains SIMD instructions, but benchmark shows no speedup over scalar — or speedup only on NTT-style loops, not on the actual field arithmetic loops where it's needed.
why: wasm SIMD requires the source language compiler to actually vectorize the inner loop. Many crypto libraries use carry-propagating representations (Montgomery, Barrett) where the inner loop has data-dependent reductions that LLVM's auto-vectorizer will not vectorize. The result: SIMD instructions appear in the binary for the loads/stores/memory shuffles, but the actual mul/add/reduce is scalar and bottlenecked on reduction latency. Only NTT butterflies with no reductions, or PLONK-style operations with delayed reduction, actually vectorize.
how_discovered: Compare scalar vs SIMD builds on a real workload: expected 2-4x, actual 1.0-1.3x. Inspect the wasm with wasm2wat and look for i32x4.mul/i32x4.add density in the hot loop — if it's mostly splat/broadcast/shuffle, the inner ops didn't vectorize. Typical waste: 1 week of 'why isn't SIMD helping.'
mitigation: Use a field representation that vectorizes: delayed reduction, packed Montgomery with batched reduction at the end of a 4-element group, or carry-less representations. Hand-vectorize the hot loops in platform-specific intrinsics or use a SIMD-friendly crypto library (e.g., blst-style for BN254, or matter-labs pairing if portable). Verify vectorization by inspecting generated wasm, not just trusting the compile flag.

pitfall_name: WebGPU readback stall hidden by triple-buffered submission
what_happens: GPU-side kernel appears fast (GPUTime small) but end-to-end proving throughput is much lower than the kernel time would suggest. Profiling shows long gaps between kernel completions that look like compute but are actually CPU↔GPU synchronization for readback.
why: WebGPU's mapAsync for reading results back requires a GPU→CPU synchronization that stalls the queue. If the algorithm pipelines stages (e.g., MSM stage 1, NTT stage 2, etc.) and each stage needs to read GPU buffers before the next, the back-pressure causes the GPU to idle. Chrome and Firefox schedule the mapAsync fence before the next dispatch's dependencies can resolve. The 'queue submit' time looks like compute in some profilers but is actually fence wait.
how_discovered: GPU timestamp queries show large gaps; CPU profile shows GPUCommandEncoder.finish / mapAsync callbacks stacked; the gap between kernel dispatch and result availability is much larger than kernel duration. Typical waste: 2-3 days chasing 'why is GPU utilization 30%.'
mitigation: Restructure the algorithm to keep multi-stage data on the GPU; only read back final results or large phase boundaries. Use multiple in-flight buffers so the GPU can rotate between them while the CPU processes the previous. For MSM, keep all bucket accumulation on-GPU; only read final accumulated points.

pitfall_name: GPU timestamp queries quantized or unavailable, distorting kernel timing
what_happens: WebGPU writeTimestamp returns values that appear quantized to ~100us or 1ms increments, or the entire timestamp query resolves with zero values on some devices/browsers, or the timestamp is in nanoseconds but represents a value with the same magnitude across many distinct kernels.
why: WebGPU timestamp queries are optional (timestamp-query feature), and even when supported, the underlying GPU timestamp counter has a resolution tied to the hardware's counter frequency. Many consumer GPUs (NVIDIA consumer, Intel integrated) quantize the counter to a coarser granularity than the kernel actually runs, especially when the kernel time is shorter than the counter period. Some mobile GPUs do not support timestamp queries at all, in which case writeTimestamp is a no-op and the resolve returns zeros or undefined.
how_discovered: A kernel that you know runs in ~10us reports as 100us or 0us. Two distinct kernels with obviously different runtimes report identical timestamps. Typical waste: half a day before realizing the timestamps aren't trustworthy.
mitigation: Run each kernel in a tight loop N times (e.g., 1000 iterations) within a single timestamp span to amplify the signal above the quantization; then divide. Validate on multiple GPUs. For correctness-critical timing, use performance.now() on the CPU side wrapped around queue.onSubmittedWorkDone() for full-submit duration, which is honest about end-to-end cost even if it includes driver overhead. Cross-check with the GPU profiler (Chrome's about:gpu trace or RenderDoc / NSight) when available.

pitfall_name: performance.now() clamped at 5ms for non-isolated contexts distorts microbenchmarks
what_happens: Repeated tiny operations (e.g., a single field multiplication) report as 5ms when they actually take microseconds. Wall-clock benchmark of an inner loop is dominated by 5ms-aligned chunks; the reported throughput is 200x slower than reality.
why: Browsers clamp performance.now() resolution to 5us (cross-origin isolated) or 100us (default) or even 5ms (Spectre-mitigated contexts, older browsers, some privacy modes, certain iframes). The clamp rounds to the next granularity boundary. A 3us operation measures as 0 if it falls within a clamp slot, then as 5ms or 100us on the next sample, giving wildly inflated or zeroed measurements.
how_discovered: Microbenchmark of a known-fast operation (e.g., a single WASM call with no I/O) reports a number like 5000us when the underlying CPU cost is microseconds. Or: tight loops of N=100 iterations report the same time as N=1000 iterations. Typical waste: hours to a day.
mitigation: Check performance.now() granularity first via a probe. Run iterations in batches large enough to exceed the clamp. Use the cross-origin-isolated resolution (5us in modern Chrome/Firefox) where possible. For sub-microsecond claims, instrument inside wasm with performance.now() substituted by a cycle counter (e.g., performance.timeOrigin + performance.now() plus BigInt(Date.now())*1e6 cross-check).

pitfall_name: JIT tier-up mid-benchmark attributed to first workload
what_happens: The first run of a proving function in a benchmark is dramatically slower than subsequent runs; the benchmark reports this as the 'cold' number and inflates the headline cost. Or: a benchmark with a small warm-up shows a sudden knee in throughput mid-run that the developer misattributes to algorithmic behavior.
why: V8/SpiderMonkey tier JIT compilation: a function starts in the interpreter, gets baseline JIT'd after ~10-100 calls, then gets optimized (TurboFan/SpiderMonkey's Ion) after type stability is proven. The first tier-up is ~10x slower than steady-state; the second tier-up is another ~2-5x. For a proving benchmark that runs each function thousands of times, the first few hundred are 'paying' for JIT compilation, and the time spent in compilation is attributed to the workload in wall-clock terms. Type instability mid-run (e.g., a polymorphic field element argument) causes deopt and a re-compile cycle that the benchmark records as the workload being slow.
how_discovered: Plotting per-iteration time shows a clear descent from cold to warm. A 'warm-up' run before measurement is conspicuously faster than the 'measurement' run. V8's --print-opt-code or Chrome DevTools' Performance > Bottom-Up shows compilation time attributed to the workload. Typical waste: 1-2 days of chasing 'why is our first measurement noisy.'
mitigation: Always run a deterministic warm-up phase (same workload, same types) before measurement begins; discard warm-up timing. Force types stable: if the prover has field elements, ensure the JIT sees only one type shape (monomorphic) by using class-based wrappers or by ensuring the same constructor is used. For absolute lowest noise, use --noopt is wrong (it disables opt and skews the other way); use steady-state measurement windows.

pitfall_name: GC pauses from JS-side intermediate buffers attributed to wasm compute
what_happens: Profiling a wasm-heavy proving workload shows major GC pauses (multiple ms to tens of ms) attributed to 'the prover' in end-to-end timing. The wasm code itself never allocates, but the surrounding JS orchestration creates many short-lived typed arrays and objects.
why: WebAssembly itself doesn't GC. But the JS that drives it (calling into wasm with buffers, constructing witness handles, parsing inputs) does. If the harness creates new Uint8Array(...) per witness fragment, or per intermediate result, the V8 young-generation fills up and minor GCs (often 1-5ms) trigger during the workload. Major GCs can hit tens of ms. Because the GC pause happens while the wasm call is in flight (or between calls), it's attributed to the wasm in wall-clock terms.
how_discovered: Chrome DevTools' Performance panel shows long yellow 'Minor GC' or red 'Major GC' blocks overlapping the wasm call blocks. Heap snapshots show a sawtooth of allocation-then-collect. performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory() shows growth. Typical waste: half a day to a day.
mitigation: Pre-allocate reusable typed array buffers in wasm linear memory and pass pointers. Avoid new Uint8Array(buf) in the hot path; use Uint8Array views over a single shared ArrayBuffer. Reuse the same JS objects across iterations. For large witness structures, use a memory pool keyed by size class.

pitfall_name: iframe sandboxing strips SharedArrayBuffer and WebGPU
what_happens: Prover embedded in a third-party iframe works in the developer's sandbox but fails or degrades silently when embedded in the customer's site. Same code, same headers, different behavior.
why: Cross-origin iframes inherit most security policies from the embedder. If the parent page is not cross-origin isolated, the iframe cannot enable SharedArrayBuffer regardless of its own headers. WebGPU availability is also gated by the embedder's permissions policy: Permissions-Policy: webgpu=(self) (or unrestricted) must be set by the parent, or the iframe gets no GPU access even if the user's browser supports it. Some embedders also block performance.now() resolution by passing allow='' instead of allowing features.
how_discovered: Test page works standalone; embedded version fails the same way as a non-isolated context. Devtools console in the iframe shows crossOriginIsolated === false despite the iframe's own headers being correct. Typical waste: 1-3 days, often confused with the customer's site being 'broken.'
mitigation: Document the embedder's required Permissions-Policy and COOP/COEP requirements in the integration guide. For the prover, detect at startup whether crossOriginIsolated and 'webgpu' in navigator are available; degrade gracefully to a single-thread SIMD path. For demo pages, ship them at a top-level origin with proper headers, never just embedded.

pitfall_name: Mobile browser tab-kill at memory pressure silently aborts long proofs
what_happens: On mobile Safari/Chrome, a proof that takes >30s to generate either completes and then the page is killed [blocked]
